the atomic force microscope can be used to image polar surfaces with atomic resolution.
the contrast of atomic force microscopy images of insulating surfaces can be inverted by changing the atomic force microscopy tip, and the contrast can be explained by electrostatic forces.
CO functionalized atomic force microscopy tips show inverted contrast compared to bare metal tips on polar surfaces.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the investigation of the interaction of a CO-terminated atomic force microscopy tip with a Cu2N island on the Cu(100) surface.
the development of new functionalized tips for atomic force microscopy.
the atomic force microscopy imaging of insulating Cu2O and Cu2N islands on Cu(100), grown in ultrahigh vacuum.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CO tip functionalization in noncontact atomic-force microscopy can invert the atomic force microscopy contrast on insulating surfaces, as long as the electrostatic force is dominant.
CO-termination of the tip inverts the contrast of the atomic force microscopy image, and this is caused by the dipole moment of the CO tip.
the atomic contrast observed on polar materials with noncontact atomic force microscopes is a consequence of electrostatic forces, which are strongly influenced by the tip apex structure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the atomic force microscope is a sensitive tool that can detect the local electric dipole moment.
the atomic contrast in atomic force microscopy is not only determined by the topography, but also by short-range electrostatic interactions.
the contrast inversion is due to the different electrostatic forces of the two tips.

atomic contrast in noncontact atomic friction microscopy images can be altered by the presence of a dipole moment on the tip.
a CO-terminated AFM tip can be used to image the atomic positions in a surface, even if the surface is polar and the tip is nonmagnetic.
